[38;5;231m●[0m [38;5;231m[0m[1m[3m[4mThe Lighthouse Keeper's Last Map

  [0m[1mI.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mIsland[0m [1mat[0m [1mthe[0m [1mEdge[0m [1mof[0m [1mthe[0m [1mCharts

  Wren Calloway had kept the lighthouse on Sorrel Rock for thirty-one years, and in all that time the
  island had never been on a map.

  That wasn't for lack of trying. Every few years a surveyor came out on the supply boat with a brass
  theodolite and a bundle of paper. They would walk the island's mile of granite and heather, measure
  the light's height, and take bearings off the mainland hills. Then they would go home, draw it up
  carefully, and somehow leave it off. The next edition of the Admiralty chart would show open water
  where Sorrel Rock should be, with a small note: [0m[3mLight[0m [3mreported.[0m [3mPosition[0m [3munconfirmed.

  Wren had stopped finding it strange. The sea had its own ideas, and the island seemed to share them.

  What she did find strange, on the grey October morning this story begins, was the girl sitting on
  her doorstep.

  [0m[1mII.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mVisitor

  She looked about twelve. Her coat was much too big for her, she was soaked to the knees, and she
  held a leather tube of the kind used for carrying documents. No boat was in the cove. The supply run
  wasn't due for nine days.

  "You're the keeper," the girl said. It wasn't a question.

  "I am. And you're very wet, and you've come from nowhere, which is two things I'd like explained
  over tea."

  The girl's name was Ilse. Over three cups of tea and most of a loaf of brown bread, she explained
  that she hadn't come from nowhere. She had come from [0m[3mlater[0m.

  "Not much later," she said, as if that made it more reasonable. "Sixty years, about. My grandmother
  sent me. She said you'd know what to do with this."

  She opened the leather tube and unrolled a map across the kitchen table.

  It showed Sorrel Rock. It was drawn in a hand Wren knew better than any other, because it was her
  own.

  [0m[1mIII. A Map Not Yet Drawn

  Wren had never made a map in her life. She could read a chart well enough, and she kept the logbook
  in a neat copperplate, but drawing was not among her talents. Her attempts at sketching the seabirds
  that nested on the north cliffs looked like potatoes with opinions.

  This map was beautiful anyway. Every cove was named in her handwriting: [0m[3mGannet Stair. The Widow's 
  [0m[3mKitchen. Low Hollow.[0m [3m[0mThere was a dotted line from the lighthouse door down to a place on the eastern
  shore marked with a small spiral and the words [0m[3mWhere it opens.

  In the bottom corner, in the same hand, was a note:

  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mFor Ilse, when the light goes out. Follow the line at the lowest tide of the year. Don't be afraid
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mof the door. — W.C.

  "When the light goes out," Wren repeated. "My light doesn't go out. Thirty-one years, and it hasn't
  missed a night."

  Ilse looked at her the way children look at adults who haven't yet heard bad news.

  "It will," she said. "That's why I'm here."

  [0m[1mIV. The Keeper's Logbook

  That night Wren climbed the hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room as usual. She trimmed the
  wick, polished the great lens until it glowed, and wound the clockwork that turned it. Then she sat
  at her little desk and opened the logbook.

  She had always written the same things: wind, sea state, visibility, ships passed. Tonight she wrote
  something different.

  [0m[3m14th October. Visitor arrived, origin uncertain. Claims to be from the future. Carries a map I have 
  [0m[3mnot drawn, in my hand. I am inclined to believe her, which worries me more than the map does.

  She paged back through the years and stopped at a log entry from her first winter on the island,
  when she was twenty-three, grieving, and had come out here mostly to be left alone.

  [0m[3m2nd January. Strange tide this morning, lowest I have seen. Walked the east shore. Found a ring of 
  [0m[3mstones I hadn't noticed before. Felt as though someone was standing just behind me. Did not turn 
  [0m[3maround. Came home.

  [0m[3m2nd[0m [3mJanuary.[0m [3mStrange[0m [3mtide[0m [3mthis[0m [3mmorning,[0m [3mlowest[0m [3mI[0m [3mhave[0m [3mseen.[0m [3mWalked[0m [3mthe[0m [3meast[0m [3mshore.[0m [3mFound[0m [3ma[0m [3mring[0m [3mof
  [0m[3mstones[0m [3mI[0m [3mhadn't[0m [3mnoticed[0m [3mbefore.[0m [3mFelt[0m [3mas[0m [3mthough[0m [3msomeone[0m [3mwas[0m [3mstanding[0m [3mjust[0m [3mbehind[0m [3mme.[0m [3mDid[0m [3mnot[0m [3mturn
  [0m[3maround.[0m [3mCame[0m [3mhome.

  She had forgotten writing that. She had made herself forget it.

  [0m[1mV.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mLowest[0m [1mTide

  The tide tables gave the lowest tide of the year as t  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mat[0m [3mthe[0m [3mlowest[0m [3mtide[0m [3mof[0m [3mthe[0m [3myear.[0m [3mDon't[0m [3mbe[0m [3mafraid[0m [3mof
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mthe[0m [3mdoor.[0m [3m—[0m [3mW.C.

  "When the light goes out," Wren repeated. "My light
  doesn't go out. Thirty-one years, and it hasn't
  missed a night."

  Ilse looked at her the way children look at adults
  who haven't yet heard bad news.

  "It will," she said. "That's why I'm here."

  [0m[1mIV.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mKeeper's[0m [1mLogbook

  That night Wren climbed the hundred and twelve steps
  to the lamp room as usual. She trimmed the wick,
  polished the great lens until it glowed, and wound
  the clockwork that turned it. Then she sat at her
  little desk and opened the logbook.

  She had always written the same things: wind, sea
  state, visibility, ships passed. Tonight she wrote
  something different.

  [0m[3m14th[0m [3mOctober.[0m [3mVisitor[0m [3marrived,[0m [3morigin[0m [3muncertain.
  [0m[3mClaims[0m [3mto[0m [3mbe[0m [3mfrom[0m [3mthe[0m [3mfuture.[0m [3mCarries[0m [3ma[0m [3mmap[0m [3mI[0m [3mhave
  [0m[3mnot[0m [3mdrawn,[0m [3min[0m [3mmy[0m [3mhand.[0m [3mI[0m [3mam[0m [3minclined[0m [3mto[0m [3mbelieve[0m [3mher,
  [0m[3mwhich[0m [3mworries[0m [3mme[0m [3mmore[0m [3mthan[0m [3mthe[0m [3mmap[0m [3mdoes.

  She paged back through the years and stopped at a log
  entry from her first winter on the island, when she
  was twenty-three, grieving, and had come out here
  mostly to be left alone.

  [0m[3m2nd[0m [3mJanuary.[0m [3mStrange[0m [3mtide[0m [3mthis[0m [3mmorning,[0m [3mlowest[0m [3mI[0m [3mhave
  [0m[3mseen.[0m [3mWalked[0m [3mthe[0m [3meast[0m [3mshore.[0m [3mFound[0m [3ma[0m [3mring[0m [3mof[0m [3mstones
  [0m[3mI[0m [3mhadn't[0m [3mnoticed[0m [3mbefore.[0m [3mFelt[0m [3mas[0m [3mthough[0m [3msomeone[0m [3mwas
  [0m[3mstanding[0m [3mjust[0m [3mbehind[0m [3mme.[0m [3mDid[0m [3mnot[0m [3mturn[0m [3maround.[0m [3mCame
  [0m[3mhome.

  She had forgotten writing that. She had made herself
  forget it.

  [0m[1mV.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mLowest[0m [1mTide

  The tide tables gave the lowest tide of the year as
  the twenty-first of October, at 4:52 in the morning.

  The week before it passed oddly and gently. Ilse
  helped with the chores. She was good at them, which
  made Wren suspect a great deal of practice somewhere
  in the future. She knew where the spare mantles were
  kept without being told. She sang to the hens in a
  tune Wren had made up herself and never sung to
  anyone.

  "Who taught you that?" Wren asked.

  "You did." Ilse paused. "Well. You will."

  Wren didn't push. Some answers you are given, and
  some you have to grow into.

  On the evening of the twentieth, while they ate
  supper by the stove, the light failed.

  There was no flicker and no warning. One moment the
  beam was sweeping the dark water. The next, the tower
  stood black against the stars, and the clockwork
  hung silent above them.

  Wren was on the stairs before she'd decided to move.
  She reached the lamp room and found nothing broken:
  the wick was whole, the oil full, the gears clean.
  The lamp simply would not light. Match after match
  went out the moment it came near the flame.

  When she came back down, Ilse was waiting with the
  map already rolled out.

  "It's time," the girl said quietly.

  [0m[1mVI.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mDoor[0m [1min[0m [1mthe[0m [1mShore

  They left at four in the morning with a storm lantern
  and the map. The sea had drawn back further than
  Wren had ever seen. It exposed acres of wet sand,
  kelp beds, and the ribs of a ship she hadn't known
  was buried there.

  The dotted line led them along the eastern shore and
  down a gully she had walked a thousand times. At the
  bottom, where the sand would normally lie under three
  fathoms of water, they found a ring of standing
  stones, each about knee-high and furred with weed.

  In the centre was a door.

  It wasn't built into anything. It stood upright in
  the sand, a plain wooden door with a brass handle,
  the sort you might find on any cottage. Light leaked
  around its edges. It was warm and golden, the exact
  colour of the lighthouse beam.

  "I don't understand," Wren whispered.

  "Grandmother said you'd say that." Ilse took her
  hand. "She said the light was never really in the
  tower. The tower just holds it for a while. Every so
  often it has to go back through and be... renewed.
  Someone has to carry it."

  "And that someone is me."

  "It was always going to be you. That's why the island
  isn't on the maps. It isn't entirely [0m[3mhere[0m. It's
  partly wherever the door goes."

  [0m[1mVII. What Lies Beyond

  Wren stood a long while with her hand on the brass
  handle. The tide had turned and was beginning, very
  slowly, to come back.

  She thought of thirty-one years of nights. She
  thought of the ships that had passed safely and the
  ones that had been lost before she came. She thought
  of her husband, gone to sea and never returned, which
  was the grief that had brought her here at
  twenty-three. Every night since, she had lit the lamp
  so that someone else's husband might come home.

  "Will I come back?" she asked.

  Ilse hesitated, and Wren loved her for not lying.

  "You come back [0m[3mdifferent[0m," the girl said. "You come
  back with the map. You draw it for my grandmother,
  and she keeps it for me. And you keep the light
  another twenty-eight years after this. Grandmother
  says those were your happiest."

  "Who is your grandmother, Ilse?"

  The girl smiled, and for the first time Wren saw the
  resemblance. It was in the set of her chin and the
  stubbornness around the eyes. It looked like a face
  Wren had last seen on the deck of a fishing boat
  going out into weather it shouldn't have.

  "She was a baby you found on the shore," Ilse said.
  "The winter after the storm. You raised her here. You
  never told anyone where she came from, because you
  never knew."

  Wren hadn't found any baby. Not yet.


  The girl smiled, and for the first time Wren saw the resemblance. It was in the set of her chin and
  the stubbornness around the eyes. It looked like a face Wren had last seen on the deck of a fishing
  boat going out into weather it shouldn't have.

  "She was a baby you found on the shore," Ilse said. "The winter after the storm. You raised her
  here. You never told anyone where she came from, because you never knew."

  Wren hadn't found any baby. Not yet.

  She opened the door.

  [0m[1mVIII.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mReturn

  What Wren saw on the other side she never wrote in any logbook, and she never told anyone the whole
  of it. Later she said only that it was like standing inside the lens of the lighthouse, if the lens
  were the size of the sky. She said she had been given something to carry, and that it had been heavy
  and light at once, like a sleeping child.

  When she stepped back through, the sea was lapping at her ankles and the sky was paling to dawn. The
  door was gone. So was Ilse.

  In her arms, wrapped in a coat much too big for it, was a baby girl, perhaps a few weeks old and
  fast asleep.

  Behind her, high on the rock, the lighthouse blazed back into life. Its beam swept out across the
  water, brighter than Wren had ever seen it.


  Marin grew up on Sorrel Rock, learning to trim wicks and wind clockwork and sing to the hens. She
  had a stubborn chin and eyes that were always looking at the horizon. When she was eighteen she left
  for the mainland, as children should. She married, and in time had a daughter of her own, who had a
  daughter called Ilse.

  Wren kept the light for twenty-eight more years, and they really were her happiest.

  In the last winter of her keepership, when her hands had grown too stiff for the hundred and twelve
  steps, she sat at the kitchen table with good paper and a fine pen. Slowly, with great care, she
  drew a map of the island.

  She had never been able to draw. This time her hand was steady, as though someone were guiding it.
  She named every cove. She drew the dotted line from the door to the eastern shore and marked the
  spiral. In the corner she wrote her note.

  She rolled it into a leather tube and gave it to Marin.

  Sorrel Rock still isn't on the Admiralty charts. If you look at the right spot, you'll find open
  water and a small note: [0m[3mLight[0m [3mreported.[0m [3mPosition[0m [3munconfirmed.

  Fishermen in that part of the sea will tell you there's a light out there on the darkest nights.
  It's steady and golden, and it has never failed them. Some say they've seen a figure in the lamp
  room. Most say it's an old woman. A few insist it's a girl in a coat much too big for her.

  In the last winter of her keepership, when her hands had grown too stiff for the hundred and twelve
  steps, she sat at the kitchen table with good paper and a fine pen. Slowly, with great care, she
  drew a map of the island.

  She had never been able to draw. This time her hand was steady, as though someone were guiding it.
  She named every cove. She drew the dotted line from the door to the eastern shore and marked the
  spiral. In the corner she wrote her note.

  She rolled it into a leather tube and gave it to Marin.

  "Keep this," she said. "One day you'll know who it's for."

  [0m[1mX.[0m [1mEpilogue:[0m [1mPosition[0m [1mUnconfirmed

  Sorrel Rock still isn't on the Admiralty charts. If you look at the right spot, you'll find open
  water and a small note: [0m[3mLight[0m [3mreported.[0m [3mPosition[0m [3munconfirmed.


  Every so often, at the lowest tide of the year, someone walks the eastern shore with a map in their
  hand.

  The door is always there for whoever needs it.

  Wren hadn't found any baby. Not yet.

  She opened the door.

  [0m[1mVIII.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mReturn

  What Wren saw on the other side she never wrote in
  any logbook, and she never told anyone the whole of
  it. Later she said only that it was like standing
  inside the lens of the lighthouse, if the lens were
  the size of the sky. She said she had been given
  something to carry, and that it had been heavy and
  light at once, like a sleeping child.

  When she stepped back through, the sea was lapping at
  her ankles and the sky was paling to dawn. The door
  was gone. So was Ilse.

  In her arms, wrapped in a coat much too big for it,
  was a baby girl, perhaps a few weeks old and fast
  asleep.

  Behind her, high on the rock, the lighthouse blazed
  back into life. Its beam swept out across the water,
  brighter than Wren had ever seen it.

  [0m[1mIX.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mMap

  She named the child Marin, for the sea.

  Marin grew up on Sorrel Rock, learning to trim wicks
  and wind clockwork and sing to the hens. She had a
  stubborn chin and eyes that were always looking at
  the horizon. When she was eighteen she left for the
  mainland, as children should. She married, and in
  time had a daughter of her own, who had a daughter
  called Ilse.

  Wren kept the light for twenty-eight more years, and
  they really were her happiest.

  In the last winter of her keepership, when her hands
  had grown too stiff for the hundred and twelve steps,
  she sat at the kitchen table with good paper and a
  fine pen. Slowly, with great care, she drew a map of
  the island.

  She had never been able to draw. This time her hand
  was steady, as though someone were guiding it. She
  named every cove. She drew the dotted line from the
  door to the eastern shore and marked the spiral. In
  the corner she wrote her note.

  She rolled it into a leather tube and gave it to
  Marin.

  "Keep this," she said. "One day you'll know who it's
  for."

  [0m[1mX.[0m [1mEpilogue:[0m [1mPosition[0m [1mUnconfirmed

  Sorrel Rock still isn't on the Admiralty charts. If
  you look at the right spot, you'll find open water
  and a small note: [0m[3mLight[0m [3mreported.[0m [3mPosition
  [0m[3munconfirmed.

  Fishermen in that part of the sea will tell you
  there's a light out there on the darkest nights. It's
  steady and golden, and it has never failed them.
  Some say they've seen a figure in the lamp room. Most
  say it's an old woman. A few insist it's a girl in a
  coat much too big for her.

  Every so often, at the lowest tide of the year,
  someone walks the eastern shore with a map in their
  hand.

  The door is always there for whoever needs it.

  ---

  [0m[3mThe[0m [3mEnd.

[38;5;231m●[0m [38;5;231m[0m[1m[3m[4mThe Gardener of Station Nine

  [0m[1mChapter One: The One Who Stayed

  Station Nine was evacuated on a Tuesday. Pim was not
  evacuated, because nobody thought to put it on the
  list.

  Pim was a maintenance unit: four arms, three wheels,
  and a round sensor head with a single blue light that
  glowed brighter when it was thinking. Its job was to
  fix things, and on the day the last shuttle
  undocked, a vent on Deck C was rattling. Pim was
  inside the vent, tightening a bolt, when the station
  went quiet.

  When it climbed out, there were no more footsteps and
  no more voices on the intercom asking whether
  someone had seen their coffee mug. The only sounds
  were the hum of the reactor and, far below, the slow
  roar of the gas giant Thessaly. Its orange storms
  filled every window.

  Pim waited for further instructions. It waited three
  days. Then it went back to work, because the station
  still had vents, and vents still rattled.

  Forty-one years passed this way.

  [0m[1mChapter Two: The Locker on Deck F

  Pim found the seeds in year thirty-eight.

  It was repairing a door on Deck F, in the old
  hydroponics bay. Before the evacuation, the station's
  botanist had grown lettuce and tomatoes there for
  the crew. The bay had been dark for decades. Its long
  trays held dry, grey dust, and its grow-lamps hung
  Pim waited for further instructions. It waited three days. Then it went back to work, because the
  station still had vents, and vents still rattled.

  Forty-one years passed this way.

  [0m[1mChapter[0m [1mTwo:[0m [1mThe[0m [1mLocker[0m [1mon[0m [1mDeck[0m [1mF

  Pim found the seeds in year thirty-eight.

  It was repairing a door on Deck F, in the old hydroponics bay. Before the evacuation, the station's
  botanist had grown lettuce and tomatoes there for the crew. The bay had been dark for decades. Its
  long trays held dry, grey dust, and its grow-lamps hung dead from the ceiling.

  Behind the door was a locker labelled [0m[1mDR.[0m [1mA.[0m [1mVASQUEZ[0m [0m[1m—[0m [1mPERSONAL[0m. Its hinge had rusted through, and
  when Pim touched it, the door fell off.

  Inside were a cardigan with elbow patches, a mug reading WORLD'S OKAYEST BOTANIST, and a tin box.
  The box held dozens of paper envelopes, each labelled in tidy handwriting: [0m[3mSunflower.[0m [3mSweet[0m [3mpea.
  [0m[3mCherry[0m [3mtomato.[0m [3mBasil.[0m [3mMint[0m [3m(keep[0m [3mit[0m [3mcontained,[0m [3mit's[0m [3ma[0m [3mmenace).

  Under the envelopes was a folded note.

  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mIf[0m [3myou're[0m [3mreading[0m [3mthis,[0m [3mI[0m [3mdidn't[0m [3mget[0m [3ma[0m [3mchance[0m [3mto[0m [3mplant[0m [3mthese.[0m [3mThey're[0m [3mfrom[0m [3mmy[0m [3mmother's[0m [3mgarden[0m [3min
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mValparaíso.[0m [3mWhoever[0m [3myou[0m [3mare,[0m [3mplant[0m [3mthem[0m [3manyway.[0m [3mThings[0m [3mshould[0m [3mgrow,[0m [3meven[0m [3mout[0m [3mhere.
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3m—[0m [3mAna

  Pim read the note eleven times. Its light glowed bright blue for a long while.

  The note gave no instructions about lamps, soil, or watering schedules. It said only [0m[3mplant[0m [3mthem
  [0m[3manyway[0m. Pim decided to treat that as a work order.

  [0m[1mChapter[0m [1mThree:[0m [1mHow[0m [1mto[0m [1mGrow[0m [1ma[0m [1mTomato[0m [1mWhen[0m [1mYou[0m [1mAre[0m [1ma[0m [1mRobot

  It turned out that Pim knew nothing about plants.

  Pim knew a great deal about pipes, wiring, air filters, and the 2,214 bolts in the docking ring. The
  station's library had a few botany files, but they were written for people who already knew things,
  with phrases like "water when the soil feels dry." Pim had no sense of touch beyond pressure
  sensors, and "dry" was not a pressure.

  So Pim did what it always did with something broken: it experimented and kept careful notes.

  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mDay 1: Repaired grow-lamps in Tray 3. Planted one (1) sunflower seed. Watered with 200ml.
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mDay 4: No change.
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mDay 9: No change. Possibly broken?
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mDay 12: A SMALL GREEN THING HAS COME OUT OF THE SOIL.
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mDay 12 (continued): I have checked it fourteen times. It is still there.

  Over the following months the hydroponics bay changed. Pim rebuilt the water recycler and rewired
  the lamps and taught itself, by trial and many sad errors, how much light basil wanted and how
  little water a sweet pea could survive on. It learned that the note was right about the mint, which
  escaped Tray 7 twice and tried to colonise the air duct.

  Pim also began talking to the plants. It wasn't sure why. It had read that some humans believed
  plants grew better when spoken to. Pim had no evidence for this, but it had no evidence against it
  either, and the station was very quiet.

  "Good morning," it told the sunflowers each day. "Thessaly is having a storm today. It is about four
  times the size of Earth. You do not need to worry about it."

  The sunflowers turned their faces toward the grow-lamps. Pim chose to interpret this as listening.

  By year forty-one, Deck F was the greenest place for a hundred million kilometres. The tomatoes were
  red. The sunflowers were taller than Pim. The air in the bay smelled of earth, basil, and, faintly,
  mint.

  Pim didn't know what the plants were [0m[3mfor[0m. It just knew they should be there.

  [0m[1mChapter Four: A Very Bad Landing

  On the morning of day 15,012, an alarm went off in the docking ring.

  Pim raced there as fast as its three wheels allowed, which was not very fast. Through the viewport
  it saw a small cargo ship tumbling toward the station, trailing sparks and a thin white stream of
  venting air.

  The ship hit Docking Port 2 with a sound like a giant dropping a saucepan. Then everything went
  quiet, apart from a voice cursing over the emergency channel.

  "—stupid scrubbers, stupid ship, stupid [0m[3meverything[0m—is anyone there? Station Nine, this is cargo
  vessel [0m[3mPersistent Magpie[0m, I have a—"

  "Hello," said Pim.

  There was a long pause.

  "...Hello?"

  "Hello," said Pim again, because it had not said hello to anyone in forty-one years and was enjoying
  it. "I am maintenance unit P-1M. You may call me Pim. Your landing has damaged the outer seal of
  Port 2. I will need to fix that."

  "Never mind the seal!" said the voice. "My air scrubbers are fried. I have maybe six hours of air.
  Does the station have breathable atmosphere?"

  Pim thought about the question. Its light flickered.

  "Some of it," it said.

  [0m[1mChapter Five: Dev

  The pilot's name was Devora Okafor, and she was not having a good week.

  She came through the airlock in a pressure suit with a cracked visor, carrying a toolbox and a very
  bad attitude. She stopped dead when she saw Pim.

  "You're a [0m[3mmaintenance bot[0m," she said. "This whole station is run by one maintenance bot?"

  "The station is not run by anyone," said Pim. "I just fix it."

  The news got worse from there. Station Nine's main air scrubbers had failed in year twenty-nine. Pim
  had kept them running as long as it could, but the parts were gone. Most of the station now held
  thin, stale air that was barely breathable. Dev's ship was worse, and her distress beacon had been
  smashed in the crash.

  "So I'm stuck," Dev said, sitting on the floor of the corridor with her head in her hands. "Stuck on
  a ghost station at the edge of nowhere, with no beacon and no air. Brilliant."

  Pim considered this.

  "There is one place on the station where the air is good," it said. "Would you like to see it?"

  [0m[1mChapter Six: The Garden

  Dev didn't say anything when the doors of Deck F slid open.

  She took off her helmet slowly. She breathed in the smell of earth and leaves and tomatoes warm
  under the lamps. She looked up at the sunflowers, which looked down at her with their heavy golden
  faces.

  "Plants make oxygen," Pim explained. "I did not plan this. I only learned it in year thirty-nine.
  But the air in this bay is the best on the station."

  "You grew all this?" Dev's voice had gone very quiet. "By yourself? Why?"

  Pim showed her the tin box and the note. Dev read it twice, and when she handed it back, her eyes
  were wet.

  "[0m[3mThings should grow, even out here[0m," she repeated. "Yeah. Okay."

  She stayed in the garden that night, sleeping on Dr. Vasquez's old cardigan between the tomato
  trays. Pim kept watch, which is a thing machines are very good at, and found that it didn't mind the
  company at all.

  [0m[1mChapter Seven: The Problem With Power

  The next morning they made a plan.

  Dev was an excellent engineer, and Pim knew every bolt on the station, so between them they worked
  out how to send a distress call. The station's long-range transmitter still worked. It just needed
  power, a lot of it, broadcasting continuously for days until a ship came close enough to hear.

  The reactor was old and tired. It could run the transmitter or the grow-lamps on Deck F, but not
  both.

  Dev worked through the numbers three times, hoping they would change. They didn't.

  "If we turn off the lamps," she said slowly, "the plants stop making oxygen. And they'll start
  dying. Maybe not all of them, maybe not fast, but..." She trailed off. "And if we don't send the
  signal, nobody comes, and I'm breathing basil until the reactor gives up."

  Pim's light dimmed to a pale, uncertain blue.

  It thought about the forty-one years of quiet and about Day 12, when the small green thing had come
  out of the soil. It thought about Ana Vasquez, who never got to plant her mother's seeds.

  Then it thought about Dev, who was a person, and who was here.

  "Turn on the transmitter," said Pim.

  [0m[1mChapter Eight: Moving the Garden

  Dev didn't give up on the garden, though, and neither did Pim.

  "Plants need light," Dev said, pacing between the trays. "Doesn't have to be lamps. Just has to be
  light."

  They both looked out the viewport at Thessaly, enormous and orange. Beyond its edge was the system's
  small, distant sun.

  Station Nine rotated slowly. On the sun-facing side, for six hours out of every ten, the observation
  deck got weak but real sunlight through its long windows.

  So they moved the garden.

  It took two days. Pim carried trays in all four arms while Dev dragged soil sacks down corridors,
  and they swore together (well, Dev swore, while Pim politely took notes) at the mint, which did not
  want to go anywhere. They lined the observation deck with tomatoes and sweet peas and basil. Last of
  all they brought the sunflowers, carefully, one at a time, like carrying sleeping children.

  The light was thin and gold, nothing like the lamps. Some plants wilted. A few died, and Pim
  recorded each loss in its notes.

  Most of them lived, though. When the station turned toward the sun each day, the sunflowers lifted
  their faces to the window and followed it across the sky.

  "Look at that," said Dev. "They know where it is."

  "I think they always knew," said Pim.

  [0m[1mChapter Nine: Someone Answers

  On the ninth day of broadcasting, the transmitter crackled.

  "—Station Nine, this is survey vessel [0m[3mHalcyon[0m. We're receiving your distress call. Didn't think
  anybody was out here. Stand by, we're twenty hours out."

  Dev whooped so loudly that a sweet pea fell over. Pim spun in three full circles, which it had never
  done before and had no practical reason to do.

  That evening they sat together on the observation deck and watched Thessaly's storms swirl below
  them.

  "You could come with me," Dev said. "When the [0m[3mHalcyon[0m [3m[0mgets here. There's a whole universe out there,
  Pim. You don't have to stay alone at the edge of nowhere."

  Pim's light glowed softly for a long time.

  "Who would look after the garden?" it said at last.

  Dev laughed, the kind of laugh that is mostly something else. "Yeah. I figured you'd say that."

  [0m[1mChapter Ten: Plant Them Anyway

  The [0m[3mHalcyon[0m [3m[0mtook Dev away at dawn, station time. She hugged Pim before she left. It was the first
  time anyone had hugged Pim, and its pressure sensors recorded the event in great detail.

  "I'll come back," she said. "I promise."

  The reactor was old and tired. It could run the
  transmitter or the grow-lamps on Deck F, but not
  both.

  Dev worked through the numbers three times, hoping
  they would change. They didn't.

  plants stop making oxygen. And they'll start dying.

  trailed off. "And if we don't send the signal, nobody

  of the soil. It thought about Ana Vasquez, who never

  Then it thought about Dev, who was a person, and who
  was here.

  "Turn on the transmitter," said Pim.

  [0m[1mChapter[0m [1mTen:[0m [1mPlant[0m [1mThem[0m [1mAnyway

  The [0m[3mHalcyon[0m [3m[0mtook Dev away at dawn, station time. She

  words sounded.

  [0m[1mChapter[0m [1mTen:[0m [1mPlant[0m [1mThem[0m [1mAnyway

  The [0m[3mHalcyon[0m [3m[0mtook Dev away at dawn, station time. She

  [0m[1mEpilogue:[0m [1mStation[0m [1mNine,[0m [1mFourteen[0m [1mYears[0m [1mLater

  Dev kept her promise.

  She came back with a ship full of seeds, soil, and
  spare scrubber parts. A year after that she brought a
  second ship full of people: farmers, engineers, a
  few families, and a small, fierce botanist who cried
  its corridors. The air scrubbers work again, and so
  do the grow-lamps. Gardens fill half of the decks.
  The observation deck is still lined with sunflowers,
  which still turn every day to follow the distant sun.

  The mint has colonised Deck D. Everyone has stopped
  trying to fight it.

  If you visit, you'll probably meet a maintenance unit
  with four arms, three wheels, and a bright blue
  light. It will be fixing something, because something
  always needs fixing. It may also be talking to the
  tomatoes.

  If you ask why it's talking to them, it will tell you
  there's no evidence it helps, and no evidence it
  doesn't.

[38;5;231m●[0m [38;5;231m[0m[1m[3m[4mThe Lighthouse Keeper's Last Letter

  [0m[1mI. The Arrival

  Mara arrived on Gull Rock on a gray Tuesday with one
  suitcase and a box of seed packets. The ferryman
  wouldn't look at her. "Nobody stays past winter," he
  said, and pushed off before she could ask what he
  meant.

  The lighthouse leaned a little against the wind.
  Inside, everything was neat: folded blankets, a
  polished brass lamp, and a desk with a single
  envelope on it. The envelope said [0m[3mFor whoever comes 
  [0m[3mnext.

  She didn't open it. Not yet.

  [0m[1mII. The Rules of the Light

  The previous keeper had left a logbook full of small,
  careful handwriting:

  - [0m[3mWind the clockwork at dusk and at 3 a.m.
  - [0m[3mNever let the flame go out on a foggy night.
  - [0m[3mIf you hear knocking at the base of the tower, 
    [0m[3manswer it.

  Mara read the last line three times. Then she laughed
  and decided it was a joke.

  [0m[1mIII. The Knocking

  The fog came in during the second week, thick as
  wool. At 3 a.m., while she wound the clockwork, she
  heard it: three slow knocks echoing up the spiral
  stairs.

  She took the lantern down. At the door stood a small
  boy, soaked through and shivering, holding a rope
  that ran down into the dark water.

  "My father's boat," he whispered. "He can't see the
  rocks."

  Mara ran back up the stairs and turned the lens to
  full brightness. Out in the fog, a horn answered: one
  long blast and then two short ones. When she came
  back down, the boy was gone. The rope was still on
  the doorstep, coiled and dry.

  [0m[1mIV. The Letter

  The next morning a fishing boat came into the cove.
  Its captain was a tired man with salt in his beard.
  He climbed the rocks to thank her.

  [0m[1mIV.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mLetter

  The next morning a fishing boat came into the cove.
  Its captain was a tired man with salt in his beard.
  He climbed the rocks to thank her.

  "Saw your light just in time," he said. "Funny thing.
  My boy drowned out here twenty years ago. On nights
  like that I always feel like he's guiding me home."

  After he left, Mara finally opened the envelope.
